title: From noticing symptoms to a breast cancer diagnosis: Black women’s experiences in the UK
official: Pathways to the diagnosis of symptomatic breast cancer among Black women in the UK: a qualitative interview study
summary:
Background and study aims
This study aims to understand the experiences of Black women diagnosed with breast cancer in the UK after noticing symptoms. Research shows that Black women are more likely to be diagnosed at a later stage and may experience delays in receiving a diagnosis and starting treatment.

This research wants to learn about women’s journeys from first noticing a symptom to receiving a diagnosis and starting treatment. Towards the end of the study, a stakeholder workshop will be held to discuss the findings and identify priorities for further research. Listening to women’s experiences will help to better understand the factors that affect these journeys and identify ways to improve care and support earlier diagnosis for Black women in the future.

Who can participate?
Women of Black African or Black Caribbean heritage who have recently received a first diagnosis of breast cancer in one of the hospitals supporting the study.

What does the study involve?
Participation involves taking part in one confidential interview with a member of the research team.  

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There is no direct benefit from taking part; however, participants may value sharing their experiences and contributing to research that could improve care for Black women with breast cancer.

Talking about their experiences may be upsetting or emotional. Participants can choose not to answer any question and pause or stop the interview at any time. If needed, the researcher can provide information about support services or suggest that they contact their GP.

Where is the study run from?
The study is run from the Department of Applied Health Sciences at the University of Birmingham, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
November 2026 to April 2028.

Who is funding the study? 
The Wellcome Trust, UK.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Patricia Apenteng, p.n.k.apenteng@bham.ac.uk

interventions.name: This study is a qualitative interview study exploring Black women’s experiences of the pathway to diagnosis of symptomatic breast cancer in the UK. 40 Black women (aged 18 years and over) who have recently been diagnosed with symptomatic breast cancer will be recruited through NHS breast clinics acr

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
The inclusion criteria for the patient interviews are:
1.	Women of Black African or Black Caribbean ethnicity with a first histologically confirmed diagnosis of symptomatic breast cancer within 6 months from search date
2.	Aged > = 18 years
3.	Diagnosed with breast cancer at a participating NHS site
4.	Ability to provide informed consent

The inclusion criteria for the stakeholder workshop are:
1.	a Black woman with lived experience of breast cancer
2.	a representative of a cancer charity or Black community organisation
3.	a healthcare professional
4.	an academic or researcher with expertise relevant to breast cancer diagnosis or health inequalities
5.	Able to speak English
Exclusion criteria:
The exclusion criteria for the patient interviews are:
1.	Women who do not identify as being of either Black African or Black Caribbean ethnicity (including mixed ethnicity)
2.	Black women diagnosed with breast cancer secondary to a primary cancer
3.	Black women diagnosed with recurrent breast cancer
4.	Black women who are acutely ill or receiving end-of-life care
5.	Black women with breast cancer detected via a screening programme
6.	Black women diagnosed with breast cancer at a non-participating NHS site
7.	Black women unable to provide informed consent
8.	Black women under 18 years of age

The exclusion criteria for the stakeholder workshop are:
1.	Those who do not meet one of the inclusion criteria (i.e., are not a Black woman with lived experience of breast cancer, a representative of a cancer charity or Black community organisation, a healthcare professional, or an academic/researcher with relevant expertise in breast cancer diagnosis or health inequalities)
2.	Those unable to provide informed consent
3.	Those under 18 years of age
